canberra.title: Do you trust the tech? Call for scrutiny of mobile detection cameras as fines top $36 million
canberra.snippet: Can Canberrans trust the technology that’s behind the ACT’s mobile device detection cameras? That’s the question being ...
canberra.content:
John Mikita (whose petition has been sponsored by Canberra Liberals MLA Peter Cain) says it’s time for the technology behind Canberra’s mobile device detection cameras – and how it’s being applied by the ACT Government – to be independently examined. Photo: John Mikita.

Can Canberrans trust the technology that’s behind the ACT’s mobile device detection cameras? That’s the question being asked in a petition calling for an independent audit of the entire infringement system.

As of 3 July, almost 58,000 infringement notices were issued by the traffic cameras for distracted driving, seatbelt and mobile device offences, equating to $36 million in fines.

Petitioner John Mikita said it’s time to ensure the system is working as intended.

“Road safety matters, and cameras can play an important role in enforcing the law. But when a system is issuing tens of thousands of fines worth tens of millions of dollars, Canberrans are entitled to know [if] that is accurate, reliable, lawful and fair,” he said.

“This should not be a case of simply asking motorists to trust the system.”

Previous questions on notice have revealed the ACT Government doesn’t know the error rate of the AI system scanning Canberra’s mobile detection cameras for road rule breakers.

This includes no information on how many infringement notices have been internally reviewed, how many were mistaken identifications or how often the system was wrong.

For a previous story, Region asked the ACT Government why it didn’t track the success/failure rates of the AI system and the human checks as a way to deliver quality assurance, whether such a mechanism was under consideration or in development, and whether an independent audit or assurance review of the system was planned. No response was received by the given deadline.

The petition has called for an examination of the technology itself and how it’s being applied in the ACT.

This would include disputed and withdrawn infringements, mistaken identifications, automated detection and classification technology, human review processes, contractor performance, quality assurance, review and appeal processes, and procedural fairness.

That’s in addition to independent testing to establish the technology’s accuracy, including false-positive and false-negative detection rates.

Mr Mikita said recent issues with the administrative and legal framework underpinning the camera’s operation strengthened the case for independent scrutiny.

“If mistakes are rare, an independent audit can demonstrate that, and strengthen public confidence,” he said.

“But if there are systemic problems, Canberrans deserve to know what they are, how many people may have been affected, and what will be done to put them right.

“Road safety matters. So does public confidence in the system enforcing it.”

The petition also called for ongoing information regarding fines, reviews, withdrawals, successful challenges, identified errors and court outcomes to be published, and for refunds or appropriate remediation if systemic errors are uncovered.

“When someone receives an infringement notice, the consequences are real,” Mr Mikita said.

“There can be a significant financial penalty and, depending on the offence, other consequences. The system imposing those penalties needs strong safeguards and proper oversight.”

The technology behind the cameras is provided by Acusensus. It developed the world’s first camera program to enforce seatbelt non-compliance and illegal mobile phone use.

According to its website, AI is used to identify images that are likely to contain offences, and whether the images should be checked by reviewers to confirm or discard each potential offence.

“Acusensus does not use generative AI and does not modify the original images captured by the cameras,” it stated.

“These images are encrypted and digitally signed on-site (at the roadside), ensuring that they cannot be manipulated in any way before being delivered to the jurisdiction responsible for the local road safety program.”

Its latest annual report stated that revenue grew from $49.6 million in FY24 to $59.4 million in FY25.

It’s currently conducting research and development to use its Heads-Up technology to potentially detect drug- and alcohol-impaired drivers, tailgating and red light offences.

Region could not locate any publicly available performance audits or reports regarding the accuracy of the technology.

But Western Australia media reported in April that about 2000 fines had to be withdrawn after an independent internal review exposed false positives.

WA Government officials maintained that, despite the issue, the multi-function camera technology was operating well overall.

An Acusensus spokesperson said the company’s mission was to ensure “everybody gets home safely, every day”, and directed Region to Access Canberra for answers to questions about program-specific results or independent testing.

“It is important to distinguish between the technology’s role and the actual issuing of an infringement. The technology’s role is to filter images and flag those likely to contain a phone or seatbelt offence,” they said.

“Images with no evidence are deleted on the roadside and never seen by a human. The technology never decides whether an infringement is issued.”

The Acusensus spokesperson added every flagged image was assessed by a human and drivers could request a review of their infringement.

“We support transparency, and as always will work with Access Canberra on any independent assessment the government decides to undertake,” they said.

The petition calling for a review of the ACT’s infringement system is open for signatures until 30 November.

canberra.title: Special sitting day at Old Parliament House scheduled for April
canberra.snippet: April next year has been chosen as the month in which for one day the whole Federal Parliament will head down the hill for a special sitt...
canberra.content:
Parliamentarians will once again debate legislation in Old Parliament House when they meet there for a special sitting next April. Photo: John Lomnicki.

April next year has been chosen as the month in which for one day the whole Federal Parliament will head down the hill for a special sitting of proceedings.

Old Parliament House will once again be home to the nation’s decision-makers as MPs and senators conduct business in the old parliament to mark 100 years since it first happened.

The building will play a special role in Canberra’s Centenary of Parliament in 2027.

Anthony Albanese will lead the celebrations, but he has quickly stressed that plenty of parliamentary work will be undertaken on the day.

“To mark 100 years since our national parliament first met in Canberra, the 48th Australian Parliament will sit for a day at Old Parliament House in April next year,” the Prime Minister said.

“The special sitting day will see Question Time, legislation and other statements return to the chambers of Old Parliament House for the first time in decades.

“In 1927, the ‘Provisional Parliament’ was opened in Canberra and our national parliamentarians continued to meet in that building until 1988.

“Learning from our democratic history and institutions is more important than ever.”

Now known as the Museum of Australian Democracy, Old Parliament House continues to play a role in Australians’ civic education.

The Joint Parliamentary Select Committee on the Centenary of Parliament in Canberra, chaired by the Member for Newcastle and Deputy Speaker, Sharon Claydon, with Member for Riverina and former deputy prime minister Michael McCormack as Deputy Chair, is advising and supporting the arrangements.

Before the building was completed in 1927, the Commonwealth Parliament sat for 26 years in Melbourne’s Victorian Parliament House, after the first parliament opened in Melbourne’s Exhibition Building on 9 May 1901.

King Charles III’s grandfather, who was at the time the Duke of York but would go on to be crowned King George VI, opened the Provisional Parliament House with a large ceremonial golden key.

In 1975, the building became the site of drama that spread around the world when Governor-General Sir John Kerr sacked then Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam.

Mr Whitlam’s “Well may we say…” speech on the steps of the provisional parliament remains part of the Australian psyche.

The building was also known for its close quarters, with numerous news ‘scoops’ having been broken simply because something was overheard in the corridors.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen noted on Saturday (17 October) that the proceedings will be cramped when parliamentarians return there for the day, but stressed that “it’s going to be great”.

“As a lover of history, I think it’s going to be a very special day,” Mr Bowen said.

“Of course, it’s going to be cramped. It won’t be a normal sort of parliamentary day.

“But it’s going to be a very special day to stand at the same dispatch boxes, you know, John Curtin and Ben Chifley and Robert Menzies and Gough Whitlam.

“I think every Member of Parliament will find that a very special day. And I hope Australians, too, recognise that Old Parliament House, together with New Parliament House, is a very important part of our history and our great achievement as one of the world’s great democracies.

“Democracy can’t be taken for granted these days, and the fact that we can celebrate our democracy and our track record as one of the world’s longest-standing democracies is a very good thing.”

No currently serving federal MP or senator sat as a parliamentarian in the old building.

Celebrating the 100th anniversary will cost taxpayers $3 million.

canberra.title: Man allegedly choked, kicked 15-year-old stepdaughter
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence. A stepfather accused of choking and kicking his 15-year-old stepdaughter...
canberra.content:
A 41-year-old man has been accused of choking his 15-year-old stepdaughter. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence.

A stepfather accused of choking and kicking his 15-year-old stepdaughter yelled at a magistrate after being told he would be kept behind bars for at least two more days.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the 41-year-old man, whose name is withheld to protect his family’s identity, returned to the Canberra home he shared with his partner and stepdaughter on Sunday afternoon (18 October).

He and the girl started arguing before he allegedly punched a window. When she confronted him over this, he allegedly kicked and choked her.

“She escaped his hold and began to call police when the man grabbed a piece of broken glass and threw it at her,” the police spokesperson alleged.

“Police will also allege that during the incident, he kicked his partner when she attempted to intervene.”

A neighbour called police, who arrived shortly afterwards.

The man faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (19 October) charged with two counts of assault and single counts of choking and property damage.

He applied for bail. This was opposed by the prosecutor, who said the girl and her mother were concerned for their safety and welfare if he was released.

The man’s lawyer, Duncan Errey of Legal Aid, said his client’s relationship with the mother could not continue in its current form. He proposed the man be released on bail to stay 100 metres away from their home.

“I’m going to detox soon, your honour, if you let me out,” his client interrupted to say.

Mr Errey said his client had been booked in for a five-day detox program at a hospital on Wednesday (21 October). Once he was released, he would try to get into a residential rehabilitation program.

Special Magistrate Sean Richter asked for evidence that the man would enter the detox program and would stay away from the mother and stepdaughter. He said if so, he would consider granting the man bail.

After speaking to his client, Mr Errey withdrew the bail application and asked to have it relisted on Wednesday so he could obtain this evidence.

“You can also ring the hospital now,” the man interrupted.

The man still wasn’t happy with the outcome and yelled again at Special Magistrate Richter about calling the hospital that day. He also threw up his hands at the judicial officer before he was led away by Correctives officers.

He will return to court on Wednesday. No pleas were entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Stronger tech and tourism ties forged on Euro trip, says Barr
canberra.snippet: Chief Minister Andrew Barr has returned from his trade mission to Europe, highlighting a swag of new links to help grow Canberra’s ...
canberra.content:
ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr with the Pearcey Foundation ACT Chief Minister’s Entrepreneur Award winners, Trellis Data founders Michael and Rachel Gately. Mr Barr says the UK and Europe offer great opportunities for Canberra’s tech sector. Photo: Andrew Barr/LinkedIn.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr has returned from his trade mission to Europe, highlighting a swag of new links to help grow Canberra’s tech industry and attract more international visitors to the national capital.

Mr Barr, who is also Trade, Knowledge Economy and Tourism and Events Minister, said engagements in Germany and the United Kingdom highlighted opportunities for Canberra businesses, researchers and institutions in research commercialisation, cyber security, digital infrastructure, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.

This week in the Legislative Assembly, the Chief Minister will outline the ACT Government’s next steps to support data centre growth, ensuring Canberra can support the nation’s digital and artificial intelligence future while protecting energy security, water resources, strategic land use and community interests.

The government says future data centre developments will be expected to deliver strong economic benefits and meet world-leading standards for renewable energy, sustainability and resource efficiency.

Mr Barr said the trip focused on creating stronger international pathways for Canberra companies through the ACT’s broader innovation ecosystem, as well as growing the number of international tourists to the national capital.

The mission met with leaders from the Hessian Ministry for Digitalisation and Innovation, Technologiepark Heidelberg, Heidelberg Innovation Park, Knowledge Quarter London, London & Partners, the Commonwealth Enterprise and Investment Council, Austrade, and major Australian banks operating in Europe.

In Germany, discussions focused on how Hesse’s digital and innovation strengths could connect with Canberra’s capabilities in cyber security, AI and quantum technologies.

Mr Barr said the Canberra Innovation Network (CBRIN), the universities, CSIRO and Canberra’s technology sector were central to the ACT’s economic future.

He said that over the next two years, the government would work with CBRIN and international partners to strengthen links with leading innovation ecosystems in Germany and the UK, attract investors and corporate partners, and support Canberra businesses pursuing opportunities in areas such as AI, cyber security, quantum technologies and the use of technology in government.

The Australia-UK Free Trade Agreement and the recently concluded Australia-EU Free Trade Agreement also opened up opportunities for local businesses.

“Our aim is to help more Canberra companies win in the UK while growing from their Canberra base, and the Australia-UK Free Trade Agreement will be key to improving access to UK customers, investment and government procurement,” he said.

Mr Barr said the goal was more high-value jobs, more private investment and more Canberra companies competing successfully in international markets.

“By 2030, we want to see several thousand more Canberrans employed in knowledge-intensive industries and hundreds of millions of dollars in additional private investment flowing into Canberra’s technology, innovation and research sectors,” he said.

CBRIN CEO Petr Adámek said the ACT tech sector’s challenge was connecting its strengths with international markets, customers, investors and partners.

“The ACT Government’s engagement with leading innovation ecosystems in Germany and the UK is an important step in opening these doors,” he said.

“We see significant opportunities to build on these relationships and help more knowledge-based businesses from Canberra turn their innovations into international commercial success.”

Qatar Airways returns to Canberra in December. The government sees it as a platform to boost international visitors to the national capital. Photo: Seth Jaworski.

The mission also aimed to attract more visitors from the UK and Europe as part of the ACT Tourism 2030 Strategy, targeting an additional 150,000 visitor nights annually by 2030 and 300,000 additional visitor nights in the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games year.

Government and VisitCanberra officials met with Tourism Australia, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Flight Centre, Trailfinders and European travel group DERTOUR to strengthen aviation partnerships, expand tourism distribution channels and increase Canberra’s share of high-value European visitors.

A key outcome of the mission was finalising a joint marketing campaign between VisitCanberra, Tourism Australia and Qatar Airways to support the return of Qatar Airways’ daily Canberra-Doha service from December and drive visitation from key European markets.

It also worked to position Canberra more strongly in future Tourism Australia destination marketing activity and Australian touring itineraries, through engagements at Australia House in London that brought together airlines, travel distributors and tourism industry leaders.

Mr Barr said the ACT Government was also working with Tourism Australia and airline partners to build longer-term opportunities with Qantas, Singapore Airlines and other carriers to support growth from Europe over the coming decade.

“The immediate focus is our campaign with Qatar Airways, but we are also building longer-term partnerships with other airlines that will help grow visitation from Europe and strengthen Canberra’s international profile,” he said.

The government aims to capitalise on a pipeline of major international events over the next decade, including the Rugby World Cup in 2027, the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup in 2028, the Ashes Cricket Tour in 2029, and the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

“These events will bring significant numbers of international visitors to Australia. Our objective is to ensure more of them include Canberra as part of a longer Australian holiday,” he said.

canberra.title: Get Halloween-ready with Canberra’s horror movie festival Yeh! Nah!
canberra.snippet: Canberra movie lovers are in for a treat just before Halloween as the ACT’s own horror film festival Yeh! Nah! kicks off next week ...
canberra.content:
Canberra’s own horror film festival, Yeh! Nah! returns for its third year with a stack of international feature-length and short films just before Halloween. Photo: Yeh! Nah! Horror Festival.

Canberra movie lovers are in for a treat just before Halloween as the ACT’s own horror film festival Yeh! Nah! kicks off next week with some of the creepiest and most terrifying movies from around the world.

With a full week of freaky films lined up, the festival’s featured night on Wednesday (28 October) will premiere the Australian-backed horror film States of Mind, directed by Che Baker, who worked on The Hobbit and Tin Tin.

The film follows a group of contestants who gather at an island retreat for what they believe is a special competition, but things turn sinister as they learn the true reason they were brought together.

After the film, viewers can join a Q&A with internationally renowned stunt performer Kiran Shah, who stars in the film and has previously worked on Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones and Star Wars.

Yeh! Nah! director Mikey J. Watson said having Kiran Shah attend the festival for States of Mind is a genuine highlight of this year’s programming and a real treat for fans.

“Kiran brings an extraordinary screen history to the festival, and his performance as Professor Manchester is central to the film’s strange, funny and unsettling energy,” he said.

“For audiences, it is a rare chance to experience a genre film with one of its stars in the room to laugh, ask questions and celebrate independent filmmaking together.

“It also reflects what we want this festival to be: a place where audiences can connect directly with the people making bold, imaginative cinema.”

While States of Mind might be the headliner, there are still plenty of other chances to see extraordinary films throughout the festival.

Opening night on Friday (23 October) at Dendy Cinema will feature 10 short films from Australia, Italy, Spain, Iran and the UK, created by some of the genre’s best emerging filmmakers.

Headlining the night will be Dance!, which follows an Israeli soldier who visits a haunted house in the Gaza Strip.

Other highlights include the Sunday (25 October) premiere of the terrifying Peruvian flick Omnipresent, a low-budget zombie thriller shot on 16mm black-and-white film.

Night five (Tuesday, 27 October) is comedy night at the Academy of Interactive Entertainment atrium, and Friday (30 October) closes the festival with awards for its best films.

Mr Watson said the eight-night festival is a true celebration of creative filmmaking in the territory, which aims to introduce more people to the genre.

“The best thing about horror is how it lends itself to creative filmmaking,” he said.

“Compared to other genres, horror is often made very cheaply, and there’s a lot of creative freedom for filmmakers to express themselves without the influence of bigger studio heads.

“Horror isn’t just linked to being scary; it can often be funny or thrilling, and not a lot of genres can get away with that.

“That summarises what this festival is about. Bringing eyes to a lot of creative works from a lot of talented filmmakers in a genre lots of people love.”

To view the entire 2026 program, visit Yeh! Nah!

australia.title: Tricky time for lunchboxes: banana shortage hits supermarket shelves after cool weather in Queensland
australia.snippet: Dearth of bananas coincides with poor apple harvest and lack of summer stone fruit Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news p...
australia.content:
A shortage of Australia’s most popular fruit, bananas, has hit supermarket shelves at a tricky time for lunchboxes, right as apple season winds down after tough growing conditions and summer stone fruit is yet to arrive en masse.

Cool weather in key Queensland growing regions has severely slowed banana production, leaving major supermarkets Coles, Woolworths and Aldi with sparse displays or very green stock.

Anton van den Berg, co-founder of the grocery delivery service Box Divvy, said demand for bananas has not fallen as significantly as it typically does for produce when supply drops.

“Many people will buy bananas no matter what, and so the demand is not adjusting, leading to shortages,” he said.

Van den Berg said major supermarkets have kept demand elevated because they rarely charge more than $5 a kilo to avoid putting off shoppers, and instead rely on thousands of other grocery lines to maintain profits.

In a note to shoppers, Woolworths said: “Recent weather in far north Queensland has slowed the growth of bananas. Stock may be limited this week, but fresh stock is arriving daily.”

Coles was contacted for comment.

Bananas are the most frequently bought fruit in Australia, according to produce data company Freshlogic, with almost nine in 10 households regularly buying them.

Apples are the next most popular fruit.

While cool weather has slowed banana growth just as the tropical fruit needs heat, unseasonably hot conditions have disrupted the temperate climates required by apple orchards, compounding the squeeze on favoured fruit.

Many countries are experiencing strains on their banana supplies, but for very different reasons.

The US has reported supply strains caused by high transport fuel costs from the war with Iran, which has affected the long-distance, refrigerated shipping required to import bananas.

While the US relies on imports, Australia grows all of its own bananas across the northern areas of Queensland, Northern Territory and Western Australia.

The Australian lunchbox conundrum may prove short-lived, with expectations banana supplies will promptly rebound.

The Australian Banana Growers’ Council said “any shortage should soon correct itself” because temperatures across affected growing regions were beginning to rise.

In the meantime, prices for stone fruit, including peaches and nectarines, are expected to drop in the coming weeks as they come into season.

Fruit sellers are still reporting healthy stock levels of navel oranges and mandarins, both of which typically start to reduce in late spring, while mango quantities are rising.

Van den Berg said mango prices were already reducing quickly and may be a suitable, albeit messier, lunchbox alternative to bananas.

“There are some kids who only eat bananas, or will only eat pink lady apples, and parents don’t have much of a choice,” he said.

“But if you do, then mangoes are definitely a better option at the moment.”

australia.title: Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff
australia.snippet: Monitoring tools common in a range of workplaces, including factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees...
australia.content:
Employers are increasingly using technology, from CCTV to keystroke monitoring, to track workers’ moves and it is being accelerated by the use of AI, the Human Technology Institute has warned.

Examples provided to Guardian Australia by the institute include a fast-food restaurant using surveillance cameras to stop workers using their phones, and AI tracking leading to a cashier warned over making a mistake once every 533 scans.

In a report released on Tuesday, the University of Technology Sydney institute said workplace monitoring tools were increasingly common in a range of workplaces, including in factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being aware of the monitoring.

Tools include CCTV, monitoring card swipes, keystroke monitoring and tracking workplace instant messaging.

The report highlighted Microsoft Teams as a common platform for workplace surveillance. The company earlier this year rolled out a tool that updates a worker’s location automatically to reflect they are in the office when they connect to workplace wifi.

Researchers at the institute were told during consultations that at one unnamed large fast-food chain, young employees were concerned their employer had put cameras in the change rooms to ensure staff were not on their phones at work. The researchers reported young people did not use the change rooms as a result.

The Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association wrote in its submission to the joint parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence that a cashier at one big supermarket received a final written warning because the AI monitoring system had flagged her making too many errors.

The error rate was reported to be 0.18%, or roughly one error per 533 items scanned.

The Human Technology Institute has called on the federal government to build privacy protections into workplace laws, given exemptions in the Privacy Act related to employee records, as well as small business exemptions, have allowed workplace surveillance to grow.

A March 2026 Minderoo-commissioned poll found 43% of Australians were aware some employers use technology including AI to monitor workers, but only 9% were aware monitoring was used in their own workplace.

Human Technology Institute co-director Prof Edward Santow said transparency over workplace surveillance was “necessary but far from sufficient”, and said the Fair Work Act should be overhauled to include a test for whether the introduction of workplace monitoring was appropriate.

“Make really clear that if you are going to be … monitoring [workers], it has to be fair and reasonable,” he said.

The minister should also be given powers to proscribe certain surveillance products that pose an “unacceptable risk” to workers’ rights, the report stated, pointing to recent federal government concern about the rise in the use of smartglasses.

“Such concern is likely to be particularly strong in a workplace context, as smart glasses could be used to covertly surveil workers,” the report stated.

It would require employers to engage with their employees on the workplace surveillance they intend to use and improve the quality of the consent obtained from employees, the report stated.

The proposed change to the law would allow employees to make privacy-related complaints to the Fair Work Commission via a dedicated complaints scheme.

The Human Technology Institute will present its findings to the joint standing committee on artificial intelligence on Tuesday, as the third week of hearings begins.

The committee will focus on AI in the workplace, with several unions to appear this week. The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, will also appear before the committee this week, as well as representatives from the CSIRO, Australian Securities and Investments Commission, the Australian Medical Association, and tech company Atlassian.

Committee member Labor senator Tony Sheldon said in a statement that workplace surveillance was becoming increasingly common and was a serious concern for employees.

“This report raises critical concerns about the impact of workplace surveillance on the privacy, health and dignity of working Australians, particularly when many employees don’t even know they’re being monitored.”

australia.title: Ellie Goulding admits error over promoting diamonds from controversial Australian mine
australia.snippet: Singer ‘mortified’ about wearing diamonds from Argyle mine at centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land The singer Ellie Gou...
australia.content:
The singer Ellie Goulding has admitted her error at having promoted diamonds at the centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land in Australia, despite having spent years campaigning on environmental issues – including the effects of mining on ancestral lands.

She appeared at a event in London earlier this month for the jewellery brand Boodles, modelling some of its newly acquired pink diamonds, some of which came from a controversial mine in Western Australia.

“Protecting the environment is a cause close to my heart. I always strive to uphold those values. Regretfully, in this instance, I fell short,” said Goulding, who was made an MBE for services to biodiversity and the climate last year. “I was not aware of the concerns surrounding the Argyle mine and I am grateful that it has been brought to my attention.

“You will certainly not see me wearing diamonds originating from the Argyle mine again. The Indigenous and local communities affected deserve better. While I am mortified to have made this error in judgment, I am letting this moment serve as a reminder and an opportunity to continue to question the status quo, to learn and do better.”

As well as serving as a global goodwill ambassador for the UN environment programme, Goulding is an ambassador for the environmental organisation WWF, which said it “takes seriously the environmental impact of mining and the effect it can have on Indigenous and local communities”.

The charity added: “Ellie is a passionate advocate for nature and human rights and has championed the rights of Indigenous peoples as a WWF ambassador. We have discussed this issue with Ellie and continue to value her support.”

A week before the Boodles event in London, it was announced the firm had bought the Argyle Pink Diamonds brand, as well as its inventory, from the mining firm Rio Tinto. A source close to Goulding suggested this timing may have led to the singer falling short of her own environmental values.

According to the Daily Mirror, which first reported the news, the Gelganyem Group, which represents the traditional owners of the land that was mined for the diamonds, has expressed concerns about the state it has been left in by the industrial processes now the mining has ceased.

The group told the paper: “Gelganyem chair Kia Dowell, a Gija woman, acknowledges Ellie Goulding’s apology and welcomes her recognition that Indigenous and local communities deserve better. She hopes it helps the public and Rio Tinto shareholders understand what is at stake at Argyle and the standard Rio Tinto’s mine closure must meet.”

The paper quoted the organisation’s representative as saying traditional owners wanted “unrestricted access without unresolved risks being left for future generations”, adding that Pfas – or forever chemicals – were one of “several technical issues traditional owners, Gelganyem and independent experts have raised”.

Rio Tinto said: “Mining at Argyle in Western Australia ended in 2020 after 37 years, and we are currently undertaking major mine closure works, including rehabilitation, with long-term monitoring and maintenance to follow. We acknowledge traditional owners as custodians of country. We are continuing to talk to them and their representatives, the Gelganyem Group, about closure, including Pfas.”

Boodles has not responded to a request for comment. The Mirror quoted a source close to the firm as saying it was not responsible for the mine itself and adding: “Boodles have bought the last batch of pink diamonds and assets from Rio Tinto including their website and Instagram account. Other jewellers have used pink diamonds in their collections.”

australia.title: ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injured
australia.snippet: Anthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked i...
australia.content:
The independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, confirmed on Monday night that a man was in custody after the alleged attack on Haines that was now being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce.

He said the motive for the alleged attack was not known, and would not comment on whether the suspect was known to police.

“Helen Haines is incredibly hard-working. She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her, she is a well-loved member of her community, and this will come as an incredible shock to that community,” Albanese said.

He said he respected her integrity most of all.

“It doesn’t mean we always agree, but I always agree that her motives are good,” Albanese said.

“Our thoughts remain with Helen Haines at this very difficult time.”

The prime minister and Victoria police said they were not aware of any recent direct threats to Haines.

Haines has represented the electorate of Indi since 2019.

Albanese later said on the ABC’s 7.30 program that while he did not want to speculate on the motivation for the alleged attack, he had repeatedly warned “the temperature has increased in recent times” in relation to politics.

He had feared that would increase the risk of political violence occurring in Australia that had been seen in other western democracies.

Albanese, who became emotional at times during the interview, said he first was told that Haines had been injured in a car accident, before being informed it was allegedly a deliberate act.

“This wasn’t an accident,” he said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also said there had been an increase in threats towards politicians.

“The year before last, we had 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against various high officeholders,” he said.

“The more recent financial year, that 951 has gone to 1,067.”

‘Our beloved Helen’

In a statement, Haines’s family confirmed that she had been injured and thanked bystanders for their assistance.

“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” they said in the statement.

“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.

“Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media.

“Please keep Helen in your thoughts.”

Haines was airlifted to hospital in Melbourne.

In a statement, Victoria police said a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, about 10km from Wangaratta, was in custody and that a knife had allegedly been found in his car. They alleged he had been detained by a passerby when he exited the car.

The statement said the woman that was struck was in a critical condition.

“Police have arrested a man after a woman was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta this afternoon.

“It is understood a white Toyota LandCruiser struck the 65-year-old woman outside an office on Murphy Street about 3.35pm.”

Police said that they were investigating as to whether it was an intentional act, and it was not known if “the parties are known to each other”.

Speaking at the scene, acting Supt Ashley Mason said it was being treated as an isolated incident.

He said that the bystanders who assisted in the arrest and with Haines should be commended for acting as they did when confronted with a “horrific tragic incident”.

It was a “dynamic incident” with an extensive crime scene, he said.

‘Deeply appalled’

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said he knew the alleged attack would be devastating for the Wangaratta community and all those Haines represented.

“I am deeply appalled by this [alleged] violent attack on Helen Haines,” he said in a statement.

“My thoughts – and the thoughts of all Victorians – are with Helen, her family, her friends, her colleagues and her community.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said t political attacks cannot be normalised in Australia.

The Liberal leader said he was “deeply saddened and distressed” and was praying for Haines and her family.

“This is a shocking day for our nation … Australians will be angry and appalled by the [alleged] attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta,” he said in a statement on social media.

In a social media post, the Nationals MP Michael McCormack said it was “such awful news”.

“Sending my love and best wishes to Helen Haines for a full and speedy recovery,” McCormack said.

‘Politically motivated violence’

Asio has in recent years repeatedly warned about the rising threat of politically motivated violence.

“Political differences, political debates and political protests are essential parts of a healthy democracy,” Mike Burgess, the Asio director general, said in 2025.

“Unfortunately, here and overseas, levels of personal grievance and frustration are growing.

“Rightly or wrongly some Australians feel dispossessed, disaffected, disenfranchised … many of the aggrieved do not necessarily espouse violent views, but may still see violence as a legitimate way to effect political or societal change.”

He added last year that although Australia’s terrorism threat level remained at probable, the system was not “designed for a situation like the one we now face”.

“We do know the environment is degrading and acts of politically motivated violence are becoming more likely than probable suggests,” he said.

“Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack.”

australia.title: Premier ‘deeply appalled’ after Indi MP Haines injured – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after Helen Haines critically injured Helen Haines, the pri...
australia.content:
Key events

  • 4h ago

    Helen Haines was scheduled to appear on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing before alleged attack

  • 4h ago

    Jess Wilson says violence has ‘no place’ in Victoria

  • 4h ago

    What we know so far

  • 5h ago

    Taylor responds to incident: ‘Australians will be angry’

  • 5h ago

    Victorian premier 'deeply appalled' by alleged attack

  • 5h ago

    Albanese says Asio, counter-terrorism force examining potential motive

  • 5h ago

    'Deeply disturbing attack': Wong, Shoebridge on Haines incident

  • 5h ago

    Victorian police say man arrested, woman in hospital with critical injuries

  • 5h ago

    PM says suspect in custody after alleged attack on Haines

  • 5h ago

    Helen Haines's family release statement

We are closing the blog for the night.

You can read the full story on the alleged attack on Helen Haines here, and an explainer here.

We’ll be back first thing tomorrow, until then, here is a rundown of what we know so far:

  • The independent MP for Indi is in a critical condition after an alleged attack involving a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, at about 3.35pm.

  • A 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee is in custody, and the alleged attack is being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce. The motive is not yet known. A knife was allegedly found in his car after he was detained by a passerby when he exited his vehicle.

  • Well-wishes towards Haines have flowed in from across the political spectrum. The prime minister held a snap press conference on Monday evening where he described Haines, who has represented Indi since 2019, as a “thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across parliament”.

  • The opposition leader, the Greens leader David Shoebridge, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and a string of independent and Nationals MPs have also sent their thoughts to Haines and her family, with many describing Haines as representing “the very best” in parliament.

  • Thoughts and prayers for Haines came amid calls to lower the political temperature in Australia. Nationals MP in the neighbouring electorate of Nicholls, Sam Birrell, said the way people were engaging had become “more angry and heated”, and added the alleged attack should be a “wake-up call”.

  • Addressing the media in Wangaratta, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said police were still investigating whether the incident was targeted. He said there was no ongoing threat to the community and nothing to indicate the parties were known to each other.

Rise in threats towards parliamentarians should ‘alarm every Australian’, Centre for Public Integrity says

The Centre for Public Integrity, an independent research institute that has had a longstanding relationship with Helen Haines, says if the alleged incident was intentional, it would be an “act of democratic violence”.

In a statement, it said it was “devastated” by the reports, describing Haines as an “extraordinary parliamentarian and an extraordinary person”.

Helen is one of Australia’s most effective and determined champions of integrity in public life. Here at the Centre for Public Integrity we have been proud to work alongside her in many campaigns … Today, we welcomed the announcement of a new National Anti-Corruption Commissioner following a transparent and merit-based appointment process, precisely the type of reform Helen has long championed.

The body said it was “shocked by the increasingly hostile environment in which Australian parliamentarians are working”.

It pointed to Australian federal police data which showed it received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance and offensive behaviour directed towards parliamentarians, high office holders and associated offices and facilities in 2025–26, an increase of 12% on the previous year.

These figures should alarm every Australian. Our democracy depends on people being willing and able to serve their communities, engage openly with the public and advocate for what they believe in, without fear for their personal safety.

‘Lower the temperature’, Nationals MP urges

The Victorian state member for Euroa, Nationals MP Annabelle Cleeland, has shared sentiments we heard earlier from the federal MP for her region, Sam Birrell, about the need to lower the temperature across the political divide.

In a statement, she said she was “shocked and appalled” about the alleged attack on Helen Haines and “violence is never the answer”.

Tonight is a reminder of why it matters to turn down the heat. Our democracy depends on people being able to disagree without fear. The way we speak about each other matters, and every one of us has a responsibility to lower the temperature of our political debate.

Similarly, Tim McCurdy, the Nationals member for the Victorian seat of Ovens Valley, which centres on Wangaratta said:

At a time like this, my thoughts are first and foremost with Helen herself and her loved ones. She is a proud representative of our community and above all, a decent human being who does not deserve this.

And Warringah MP Zali Steggall, who sits next to Helen Haines in Parliament and has worked with her since 2019 when they were both elected, says she is “shocked and devastated” by the news. She said:

She is a wonderful, caring, smart and wise friend and amazing representative for her community. I am thinking of Helen and her wonderful family.

Benita Kolovos

Helen Haines ‘adored by her community’, Animal Justice party MP, Georgie Purcell, says

The Animal Justice party MP, Georgie Purcell, whose Victorian upper house region of northern Victoria overlaps with parts of Helen Haines’s seat of Indi, has described the independent as an “absolute powerhouse” who is “adored by her community”.

This shocking [alleged] attack will rattle the entire nation, but especially the people of Indi. And while a motivation is yet to be confirmed, I know this will also send chills down the spines of women in parliaments across the country, as well as candidates contesting the Victorian state election.

She says being a woman in politics “changes the way you move throughout the world”, including where they park your car, the route to drive home or if they hold public events or keep their office doors locked. Purcell went on:

For many of us, the news coming out of Wangaratta this evening is our worst nightmare. Only weeks ago I spoke in parliament about the escalating safety fears of women in public life – just as I have countless times before. We cannot continue to encourage women to put themselves forward for public office while failing to address the growing threats to our safety.

Our parliaments and communities are better off because of people like Helen – a nurse and midwife who has advocated for regional Victoria relentlessly. We will all be poorer for it if people like her cannot safely participate in our democracy.

Helen Haines was scheduled to appear on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing before alleged attack

The host of the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing Patricia Karvelas has just told the public broadcaster that Helen Haines was due to appear on her program before the alleged attack occurred.

Visibly emotional, Karvelas said Haines was to speak about the National Anti-Corruption Commission, for which she has been a long-time advocate, prior to the incident occurring.

She couldn’t do the interview … because she was [allegedly] brutally attacked. She couldn’t do her democratic job … because of this. It’s horrific, I think, and I’m quite upset by it.

Nationals MP in neighbouring electorate says alleged attack should be a wake-up call

The Nationals member for Nicholls, Sam Birrell, is appearing on ABC News. Birrell’s electorate neighbours Indi and shares a long border.

He says he is feeling “shocked”, having recently seen Helen Haines at an event in Euroa with the governor general.

Helen is a friend, we have our political differences but share a long electorate border … Helen Haines is not a divisive figure … She’s a regional MP … just a local hard-working MP like I try to be and a lot of my colleagues. To have something like this occur in Wangaratta … That’s the particular element that has sent a shock wave for me but also my colleagues.

Birrell says he won’t change his conduct in light of the alleged attack, adding “we don’t hate each other in parliament”, but points to rising anger he’s seen in the community.

We see each other as colleagues … It’s a real feature of the Australian democracy that you can [come up to the local MP]. I don’t want to see that lost.

I think we’ve all noticed the way people engage on social media and with our offices … has become more angry and heated. I agree with the prime minister that we need to take the temperature down.

Sarah Basford Canales

Neighbouring MP, David Farley, wishes Helen Haines the ‘tenacity and strength of Hercules’ to recover

Across the Murray river in the neighbouring federal electorate of Farrer, One Nation MP, David Farley, said he was at home digesting the news.

In a statement, he said:

Wishing Helen Haines the tenacity & strength of Hercules to recover from her horrific injuries.

Helen is the best of all of us, great representative, tenacious politician, genuine and authentic Australian.

Our prayers across Farrer are with Helen and family tonight.

We brought you the statement from One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, earlier, who said “violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia”.

Jess Wilson says violence has ‘no place’ in Victoria

Benita Kolovos

The Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, says she’s deeply shocked about the “terrible” alleged attack on Haines. Her statement reads:

My thoughts are with Helen, her family, friends and staff at this incredibly difficult time. I know Victorians everywhere will be hoping for her recovery.

I want to thank the bystanders who rushed to help, along with Victoria Police, paramedics and the medical professionals caring for Helen.

The circumstances of this [alleged] attack are deeply concerning, and it is important that police are given every opportunity to establish exactly what happened. Violence of this kind has no place in our state.

She added that she had spoken with premier Ben Carroll this evening and the duo are “united in our resolve that such extreme acts cannot be tolerated in a democratic society.”

Wilson said:

Helen is a dedicated and decent person who has spent years standing up for her community. Right now, our thoughts are with her and those closest to her.

The deputy premier of Victoria, Gabrielle Williams, also threw her support behind Haines.

In a statement posted to social media, she said she was “deeply shocked” and her heart went out to Haines, her family and friends.

Helen is a fierce advocate for her community in Indi, and I know they’ll be feeling this deeply as well.

Spender says many have feared a violent incident against an Australian politician

Spender says many people have feared that there would be a violent incident against an Australian politician. Police are still investigating whether the incident involving Helen Haines was an intentional act.

Earlier this evening, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said the number of reports of harassment and threatening behaviour against MPs and high office holders had increased since last year.

Spender tells ABC’s 7.30:

Look, I think we’ve seen an increase in, in violent language and also, you know, sort of some of the actions of jostling and other kind of actions against politicians. And I think many people have feared that there would be some sort of violent incident against Australian politicians. And I think this is of huge concern because I think we take pride in the fact that in Australia, you know, politicians are just like anybody else.

Asked about incidents overseas, including in the UK where multiple MPs have been killed in recent years, she says everyone needs to tone down their language.

You can’t control everything, including you know, and we don’t know the circumstances of this. But you know, we have always, we’ve done better in this country and we have to continue to do better.

Frankly, you know, the sort of abuse of people in our hospitals, in our supermarkets. This is part of a trend that we, I think as a country, not just as politicians. We need to step up for and say, you know what? You know, we behave in a way that we don’t want to see this sort of violence in language or violence in attitude. And I think we collectively are responsible for that.

What we know so far

If you’re just joining us, here’s a recap of what we know so far after the alleged attack on the independent member for Indi, Helen Haines.

  • Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, regional Victoria, at about 3.35pm.

  • A 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee is in custody, and the alleged attack is being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce. The motive is not yet known. A knife was allegedly found in his car after he was detained by a passerby when he exited his vehicle.

  • The prime minister, the opposition leader, the Greens leader David Shoebridge, One Nation head Pauline Hanson and politicians across the parliament have sent their thoughts and well wishes to Haines and her family.

  • In a snap press conference on Monday evening, Anthony Albanese described Haines, who has represented Indi since 2019, as a “thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across parliament”.

  • Addressing the media in Wangaratta, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said police were still investigating whether the incident was targeted. He said there was no ongoing threat to the community and nothing to indicate the parties were known to each other.

Haines is ‘really inspirational’, says Spender

Allegra Spender, who sits on the crossbench with Helen Haines, calls her one of the most outstanding people in parliament.

She tells ABC’s 7.30 Haines interrogates issues thoroughly but with enormous respect.

Spender says she found out about the incident from her colleagues.

Helen is the best of us. Like, Helen is one of the most outstanding people in parliament.

She’s really inspirational. I often go and talk to her, particularly if I’m looking at regional and rural issues and get her perspective on what her community thinks. But also, you know, … You see her with ministers, for instance. She takes the work incredibly seriously. She interrogates the issues very seriously, but with enormous respect and with a very civilised approach.

1 of 3
